report:
Based on this research, I can confirm your conclusion is well-supported by the evidence.

## Summary

**No, hydroxychloroquine does not reduce mortality from COVID-19 — and in some contexts it may increase risk of death.** This conclusion is supported by the largest, most rigorous randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and meta-analyses conducted during the pandemic.

**Key evidence:**

1. **RECOVERY Trial (UK)** — one of the largest RCTs (1,542 hydroxychloroquine patients vs. 3,132 usual-care controls), published in NEJM, found no mortality benefit and the arm was halted for futility (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926).

2. **WHO Solidarity Trial** — a multinational RCT of ~10,000 hospitalized patients similarly found hydroxychloroquine had no effect on survival, leading WHO to discontinue that treatment arm (https://gitnux.org/covid-lies-and-statistics/).

3. **International collaborative meta-analysis (Axfors et al., Nature Communications, 2021)** — pooling published and unpublished RCT data, this rigorous analysis found hydroxychloroquine treatment was associated with **increased** mortality in COVID-19 patients, with no evidence of benefit (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z).

4. **Systematic review/meta-analysis (PMC, 2021)** — corroborated that hydroxychloroquine was not associated with reduced mortality, and combination with azithromycin significantly increased mortality risk (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8220439/).

**Caveats:** Some early observational studies and non-randomized reports suggested benefit, but these were generally smaller, subject to confounding, or later found to rely on flawed data. Randomized trials — the gold standard for causal inference — consistently show no mortality benefit, and some show harm, especially combined with azithromycin.

**Conclusion:** The weight of high-quality RCT evidence strongly supports that hydroxychloroquine does not reduce COVID-19 mortality and may be harmful in some regimens.
